name: Carla Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at St Anne's, a charity clinic run by the church in our small town, and we see anyone who walks in, a lot of them without much money. The waiting room is full by half eight: young mums, farm workers, older people who can't get to the hospital in the city. I like knowing that the people we see would otherwise go without. What wears me out is the budget, because the charity counts every bandage, and there's always more need than money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools at St Anne's?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A little. The charity was given a free AI tool that drafts letters and summarises hospital reports, and I use it a few times a week when I'm behind. I waited until the older doctor, Dr Patel, had tried it for a few months and said it was safe. My husband Daniel is an electrician, and he laughs that I'm slower with technology than his seventy-year-old customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I expected, and that's fine with me. At the clinic we'd keep using the letter tool and get on with it. I'd say to friends at church that good care was never about gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means our own worries carry on. Daniel started his own electrical business this spring, and we put all our savings into his van and tools, so we have maybe three weeks of money. The charity pays less than other clinics, and there's nothing else nearby, so I'm staying put.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and use the letter tool when I'm behind. We'd keep a tight budget until Daniel's business finds its feet, so no holiday this year. And we'd still try for a baby next year, as planned, because that's what we've been praying about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A bit stretched for money, but hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Daniel has a slow month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then my wage covers everything, which it just about can if we're careful. My mother would help with food if we asked, and the church has a fund for families in trouble, though I'd be embarrassed to use it. We'd manage, but it would be tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still try for a baby next year. Does money make you hesitate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Some friends say wait until you have savings. My mother had four of us with less, and I believe things work out if you work hard and look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it could help a charity like ours stretch the budget, if it's done carefully. At the clinic I'd suggest we wait and see what works elsewhere before going further. At church I'd say the human side of care matters most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think St Anne's might use it to get by with fewer doctors. The board counts every penny, and if AI handles letters, reports and booking, they may not replace Dr Patel when he retires next year. My own job is probably safe, but I'd be doing more for the same pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the letter tool properly and the new booking system once Dr Patel and the nurses had tried it. I'd take over the books for Daniel's business in the evenings, using AI to do the invoices, so he can spend more time on jobs. And we'd still try for the baby, but maybe a few months later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened, just aware that things are shifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is Daniel's work affected in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, I think. Robots come slowly to hands-on work, and everyone wants new wiring, chargers and solar panels. My husband the electrician might end up being the steady earner, which he'd enjoy teasing me about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do more for the same pay. Would you push back on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gently. I'd ask the board for a small rise if I'm covering for Dr Patel. But it's a charity, and I knew that when I joined.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and families and communities will be left to pick up the pieces. At church I'd say we need to look after each other. I wouldn't say much online; that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think by 2028 the clinic wouldn't need me for the thinking work, and that's most of what they pay a doctor for. I'd have hands-on examinations until robots come around 2031, but a charity would rather pay a nurse. Daniel's work lasts longer, but his business is only months old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd put the baby on hold, which would break my heart a bit. I'd look for any job that needs a person in the room, maybe the care home or the hospice, because those are hands-on. We'd cut everything except the van payments and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake thinking about all the women I see at the clinic, and about our own plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel about the baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we wait two years, not forever. He'd agree, because he's patient, but I'd see it in his face. We'd pray about it together that night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you turn for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, my mother and Daniel's parents. Then the church community, who've helped others before. I'd only go to the government as a last resort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still fast, but it's enough to prepare a little. At the clinic I'd suggest we plan together. At church I'd talk about what families can do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have time to move into women's health and baby care, which is hands-on. By 2031 the thinking work is gone, but antenatal checks and baby clinics need a person until robots come around 2034. That fits my life too, if we have our own child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a course in women's and children's health next year, if St Anne's would split the cost. I'd learn the AI tools properly, since I'd be using them for the paperwork side. And we'd save toward three months of money before the baby comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's easier to face when I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask the charity board first, because they'd benefit. If they can't, I'd use money from doing Daniel's books. It would take a year, but it's doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry that's only buying a few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. By 2034 even baby clinics may change. But by then our child would be a toddler, and I'd have some savings and Daniel's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, and people shouldn't panic. At the clinic I'd say we've time to do this properly. At church I'd say families should plan sensibly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be all right. Daniel's business would be established, I'd have retrained in women's and children's health, and we'd have a child or two. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking work goes and forty when robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd try for the baby next year as planned. I'd do the women's and children's health course in a couple of years. And we'd put a little into Daniel's business each year, maybe a second van and an apprentice, because hands-on trades last longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. It feels like normal life with a big change at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprentice. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because young people need a trade, and Daniel learned his from an old electrician who took a chance on him. I'd rather we did that for someone than wait for a government scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children's future. They'd grow up in a world where machines do most thinking work. I'd want my children to learn a trade as well as school, like their father.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would mean putting off our family and Daniel's business is too new to carry us. What would help is time and a fair chance to retrain without losing my wage, and some support for small businesses like Daniel's. Family and church would do the rest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the patients we see. Many of them don't have smartphones or reliable internet. If care goes all digital, the people at St Anne's charity clinic are the ones left behind.

headlineQuote: If care goes all digital, the people at St Anne's charity clinic are the ones left behind.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old** doctor at St Anne's, a church-run charity clinic in a small town.
She's married to **Daniel**, a new self-employed electrician, and their savings went into his van.
She uses AI **now and then**, after a senior colleague tested it.
Fast AGI **alarms** her mainly because she'd put off having a baby.
With more time she'd retrain in **women's and children's** health and invest in Daniel's trade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, as it means **delaying a family** with a business too new to carry them.
whatWouldHelp: A **fair chance** to retrain without losing her wage, plus support for **small businesses**.
